item.title: Shared stories fuel closer cross-Strait film cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
Shared stories fuel closer cross-Strait film cooperation BEIJING, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- Closer cooperation was a common aspiration at a cross-Strait film and television forum in Beijing on Thursday. More than 170 industry representatives gathered to discuss ways to work together and make better films. For many participants, the cultural ties shared by audiences on both sides offer a strong foundation for future cooperation. "On many themes explored in film, audiences on both sides share similar emotions and a common cultural understanding," said screenwriter Ho Hsin-Ming from Taiwan. He cited a homecoming scene set around the Chinese New Year in a film he worked on as a screenwriter. "Audiences across the Strait understand what returning home for the Chinese New Year means. That cultural connection needs no explanation," he said. Such connections are creating new opportunities in the film and television industries. Zhang Yan, vice president of the China Taiwan Hong Kong Film Research Association, noted that cooperation now extends beyond films to include television dramas and short-form online series. Measures unveiled by the mainland in April further opened up opportunities for filmmakers from Taiwan, including support for film and television works portraying family ties and everyday life across the Strait, as well as opportunities for Taiwan's industry professionals to participate in mainland short-form series. Director Wu Chen-Ya from Taiwan said he had seen the benefits firsthand. A film in which he acted was successfully released in the mainland in April. "Policies supporting and encouraging high-quality films from Taiwan have brought real benefits to filmmakers from Taiwan," he said. The interest goes both ways. A film producer from Taiwan who has helped bring about 10 mainland film and television productions to Taiwan said audiences there had responded enthusiastically to mainland films at cross-Strait film festivals. Recent film releases have highlighted the strong appeal of films across the Strait. The film "The Pig, the Snake and the Pigeon" from Taiwan earned more than 600 million yuan (about 88.5 million U.S. dollars) at the mainland box office in 2024. In August this year, tickets for two screenings of the mainland film "Dear You" in Taiwan sold out within five minutes. Looking to the future, participants also focused on AI, which is rapidly changing how films and television programs are produced around the world. "The mainland has abundant AI resources and generative-model capabilities, while Taiwan has extensive experience in film and television production," Wu said. "By combining these strengths, we can enhance the competitiveness of Chinese-language productions in international markets." Despite the excitement over new technology, Wu emphasized that the essence of filmmaking remains unchanged. "Although AI is giving filmmaking more technological tools, movies are still ultimately about people's stories," he said. "I hope filmmakers on both sides can work more closely to explore our shared history and culture and tell more moving stories across the Taiwan Strait."

item.title: Mainland to promote peaceful cross-Strait relations, integrated development: official
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
Mainland to promote peaceful cross-Strait relations, integrated development: official WUHAN, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- A senior Chinese mainland official said on Thursday that the mainland will firmly promote the peaceful development of relations across the Taiwan Strait and integrated cross-Strait development. Peng Qing'en, deputy head of the Taiwan Work Office of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and the Taiwan Affairs Office of the State Council, made the remarks at the opening of a two-day symposium on cross-Strait relations in Wuhan, capital city of central China's Hubei Province. Peng called on people across the Strait to work together to firmly oppose "Taiwan independence" separatism and external interference, safeguard the shared homeland of the Chinese nation, and work together toward national reunification and national rejuvenation. More than 160 experts, scholars and other participants from across the Strait are attending the symposium. They noted that the mainland has successfully embarked on a path of modernization marked by robust economic momentum and vibrancy, offering broad prospects for cross-Strait relations and national rejuvenation. People on both sides should expand exchanges and cooperation in all fields and safeguard peace and stability across the Strait, they added. The Taiwan question is a scar left by a full-blown civil war fought between forces led by the CPC and the Chinese Kuomintang (KMT) about eight decades ago. In 1949, the remnants of the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, and the People's Republic of China was founded under the leadership of the CPC. This unresolved civil war, combined with foreign interference, has left the two sides of the Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation. However, the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed.

item.title: Scholars: Natl identity key to bolstering ties
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
Scholars: Natl identity key to bolstering ties Scholars from Taiwan and the mainland stressed at a seminar that a sound sense of Chinese national identity is fundamental to the development of cross-Strait relations, while expressing concern about the Democratic Progressive Party authorities' efforts to distort that identity by promoting "Taiwan independence" separatism. Addressing the 2026 Cross-Strait Relations Seminar, which opened on Thursday in Wuhan, Hubei province, Peng Qing'en, deputy director of the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, called on Taiwan compatriots to uphold the greater national interest and recognize the broader historical trend. He also urged them to jointly oppose "Taiwan independence" separatism and external interference and safeguard the common homeland of the Chinese nation. The two-day seminar was organized by the mainland-based cross-Strait relations research center and brought together more than 160 scholars and experts from both sides of the Taiwan Strait. Wang Yingjin, director of the Research Center for Cross-Strait Relations at Renmin University of China, said a sound sense of national identity is the first step in advancing cross-Strait relations and an important prerequisite for fostering emotional affinity between people on both sides. Yang Yizu, vice-president of the All-China Federation of Taiwan Compatriots, said that, since Taiwan is part of China's territory, people in Taiwan originally had no issue with their identification with China. He said separatist forces on the island have sought to construct a "Taiwan independence" identity through policies, which he described as false identification. "Identification with national reunification is natural, while identification with 'Taiwan independence' is artificial," Yang said. Chi Hsing, president and publisher of The Observer, a Taiwan-based magazine, said "different systems are not an excuse for secession". She said people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait form a community with a shared future and that Taiwan compatriots should uphold the tradition of patriotism reflected in their shared historical memory. "The status quo across the Taiwan Strait is a transitional phase towards national reunification," Chi said. Referring to the island's "constitution", whose preamble states that it is intended to "meet the needs before national reunification", she said Taiwan has only the option of pursuing reunification, not "Taiwan independence". Experts at the seminar noted that the mainland's continuous development and progress has contributed to a growing sense of identification with China among people on the island. They also called on people in Taiwan to gain a better understanding of the mainland. Ting Jen-fang, president of the south Taiwan cross-Strait relations association, said new forms of traditional Chinese culture have strong appeal among young people in Taiwan. He cited popular works such as the dance drama A Tapestry of a Legendary Landand the television series Pursuit of Jadeas examples, saying they are opening up new avenues for cross-Strait cultural exchange. Yang Kai-huang, director of the Cross-Strait Research Center at Ming Chuan University in Taiwan, encouraged people in Taiwan to experience the mainland's technological development, including the application of smart technologies in daily life and healthcare. Such developments, he said, offer a glimpse into future models and could also help strengthen a sense of identification.

item.title: DPP accused of spreading lies to curb ties
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-20
DPP accused of spreading lies to curb ties Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party authorities have spared no effort to restrict and obstruct exchanges across the Taiwan Strait, fearing that the "information cocoons" they have created will continue to be punctured, a Chinese mainland spokesperson said on Wednesday. At a regular news conference, Zhu Fenglian, a spokeswoman for the Taiwan Affairs Office of the State Council, said the DPP authorities have resorted to tactics including suppression, intimidation and rumormongering, while the island's "mainland affairs council" has been at the forefront, becoming a "stumbling block" to cross-Strait exchanges and interactions. "They have tried every possible means to prevent people on both sides from visiting each other and maintaining close ties," she said. Zhu made the remarks in response to recent comments by the "mainland affairs council" on a new regulation on exit and entry administration issued by the State Council, China's Cabinet, which will take effect on Sept 15. Taiwan's "mainland affairs council" claimed that the regulation could affect Taiwan residents who invest or work in the technology sector on the mainland and urged them to be alert to the purported "risks". Zhu said the regulation will help safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait in their exchanges and create a better law-based environment for Taiwan compatriots visiting the mainland. Reassuring Taiwan residents that they have no need to worry about risks when traveling to the mainland, Zhu accused the DPP authorities of deliberately spreading alarm with ulterior motives. "Faced with the unstoppable tide of cross-Strait exchanges and interactions, what the DPP authorities fear most is that the information cocoons they have created will continue to be punctured and the false 'Taiwan independence' narratives they have constructed will continue to be exposed," she said. "That is why they have resorted to making such reckless and unfounded statements." Zhu also condemned the DPP authorities for continuing to delay allowing mainland residents to travel to Taiwan due to their "Taiwan independence" stance, saying the policy has artificially severed the tourism market across the Taiwan Strait. "This will only cause Taiwan to miss out on the enormous potential of the mainland's tourist market," she said. According to local media reports, Taiwan recorded a tourism deficit of 6.36 million person-trips in the first half of this year. Industry representatives on the island attributed the shortfall mainly to the continued absence of regular travel by mainland tourists to Taiwan, calling on the DPP authorities to reopen the island to mainland tourists as soon as possible. The DPP authorities have also required civil servants in Taiwan to submit applications when traveling to the mainland to visit relatives, along with contact information for their mainland relatives and friends, drawing criticism from the public. Zhu said the move was a further infringement on the personal privacy of Taiwan residents. "They aim to prevent Taiwan people from visiting the mainland, while what they fear is that more people will see through their true motives of deceiving and inciting people with lies to pursue political self-interest by promoting 'anti-China' and 'resisting China'," she said. Zhu said the mainland has been actively promoting exchanges between people on both sides. From Aug 24 to 28, relevant youth organizations from both sides will jointly host a cross-Strait youth exchange event in Shanghai, as part of efforts to implement the institutionalized platform for two-way youth exchanges between the Communist Party of China and the Chinese Kuomintang, outlined in 10 policy measures released by the mainland in April.

item.title: 2nd Lutai Youth Zhucheng-School Guqin Exchange Gathering & Cross-Strait Guqin Masters Concert Held in Zhucheng, Weifang
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-20
2nd Lutai Youth Zhucheng-School Guqin Exchange Gathering & Cross-Strait Guqin Masters Concert Held in Zhucheng, Weifang Source: Taiwan.cnUpdated: 2026-08-20
Aug 20(Taiwan.cn)—On the morning of August 16, the 2nd Lutai Youth Zhucheng-School Guqin Exchange Gathering and Cross-Strait Guqin Masters Concert themed “Dragon Rhythms of Silk Strings, Bonds Across the Taiwan Strait” took place in Zhucheng, Weifang. Under the banner of “Seven-Stringed Instrument Inherits Cultural Heritage, Both Sides of the Strait Share Melodies,” the event brought together more than 100 guqin masters, enthusiasts and youth representatives from across the Taiwan Strait. Using the guqin as a medium and music to convey affection, the event featured gentle, time-honored string music to bridge cross-Strait cultural heritage and celebrated the fraternal bonds between compatriots across the Strait. At the venue, guests from both sides jointly plucked the strings, producing clear, melodious guqin tones. During the performance session, renowned guqin artists from the Chinese mainland and Taiwan took the stage in succession to deliver heartfelt renditions. Diverse guqin styles were showcased side by side, presenting a feast of guqin art rich in cultural depth and heartfelt emotion. Pieces of the Zhucheng school feature robust tones and bold expressive qualities, fully embodying the profound spirit of Qilu ritual and music culture. The Mei-An guqin repertoire, which originated in Zhucheng and gained popularity in Taiwan, boasts graceful, delicate and lingering melodies, reflecting the refined tastes of traditional literati. Classic works including "Moon Over Mountain Pass," "Flowing Water," "Parting at Yangguan," "Lament of Changmen," and "Night Thoughts by the Window" were performed in succession. Performances alternated between guqin-xiao duets and two-guqin ensembles, producing pure, mellow string sounds with lasting resonance. The closing piece "Homecoming" conveyed sincere emotions and profound significance, vividly illustrating the deep kinship rooted in shared bloodline and cultural heritage that binds compatriots across the Taiwan Strait. As young people from both sides played the guqin, discussed techniques, and bonded through music, they gained a profound understanding of their shared Chinese cultural origins, jointly composing an era-defining melody for cross-Strait unity and shared progress. This series of exchange activities lasted six days, featuring special performances by young guqin players from both sides of the Strait and salons exploring the origins of guqin culture. These sessions provided a platform for guqin masters and young enthusiasts to gather, exchange ideas and learn from one another. During the event, the Taiwan youth study-tour group embarked on immersive study tours across Weifang, Qingdao and Jining. They admired the splendid landscapes of Shandong, experienced the essence of Confucian culture, appreciated the charm of intangible cultural heritage, and gained deep insight into Shandong’s time-honored historical legacy and dynamic high-quality development. Through varied forms including on-site visits and interactive exchanges, the event shared cultural stories of shared roots and spiritual affinity across the Taiwan Strait, and garnered strong youthful vitality for deepening Lutai cultural exchanges and advancing cross-Strait integrated development. (Jointly reported by Taiwan.cn and the Taiwan Affairs Office of Weifang) Related Stories

item.title: Publicizing Cross-Strait Policies, Deepening Cross-Strait Bonds
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-20
Publicizing Cross-Strait Policies, Deepening Cross-Strait Bonds Source: Taiwan.cnUpdated: 2026-08-20
Aug 20(Taiwan.cn)—Recently, to further publicize cross-Strait laws, regulations, principles and policies, and build broad consensus for cross-Strait integrated development, the Taiwan Affairs Office of Longting District, Kaifeng City launched a community-based cross-Strait publicity and education campaign in Wuchaomen Community. The initiative aims to embed the concept that “people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait as one family.” into residents’ daily lives and root it deeply in public’s hearts. At the event, staff members from the Taiwan Affairs Office of Longting District cited Henan Province’s Implementation Opinions on Promoting Cross-Strait Economic and Cultural Exchanges and Cooperation. Focusing on pressing concerns of Taiwan compatriots and their family members residing in the district, they explained central, provincial and municipal Taiwan-related policies and the current cross-Strait situation in plain and accessible language. They delivered detailed briefings on preferential measures covering employment, entrepreneurship, social welfare, and children’s schooling that benefit Taiwan compatriots and their relatives. Meanwhile, residents were informed about how to guard against fraud in cross-Strait affairs. This helped the public fill gaps in their understanding of relevant policies. Going forward, the Taiwan Affairs Office of Longting District, Kaifeng City will keep innovating outreach approaches and diversifying communication channels. It will effectively address the real needs of local Taiwan compatriots and their family members, further consolidate the grassroots foundation for cross-Strait integrated development, keep highlighting the central theme of “we on both sides of the Taiwan Strait are one family,” and mobilize broader grassroots support for advancing the peaceful development of cross-Strait relations. (Jointly reported by Taiwan.cn and the Taiwan Affairs Office of Kaifeng) Related Stories

item.title: Cross-Strait Red Cross Youth Summer Camp Kicks Off in Guiyang
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-20
Cross-Strait Red Cross Youth Summer Camp Kicks Off in Guiyang Source: Taiwan.cnUpdated: 2026-08-20
Aug 20(Taiwan.cn)—Recently, the opening ceremony of the 2026 Cross-Strait Red Cross Youth Humanitarian Tour Summer Camp was held at Tuyunguan in Guiyang. Integrating three core components — cultural study tours, field visits, and public-welfare practices — the summer camp provides a high-quality platform for in-depth, face-to-face exchanges between young students from Taiwan and their counterparts in Guizhou. During the camp, young participants from both sides of the Taiwan Strait toured Guizhou to see the remarkable achievements of Guizhou in new-era economic and social development, ecological progress, ethnic cultural heritage, and rural revitalization. They also gained first-hand knowledge of the Red Cross operational systems covering first aid, humanitarian assistance, public welfare and charitable activities, as well as youth volunteer services, thereby gaining a more comprehensive understanding of the Red Cross cause and public-welfare system on the Chinese mainland. Through discussions on public welfare initiatives, mutual learning, and experience sharing, young people from Guizhou and Taiwan forged profound friendships. The event fostered cultural identity among cross-Strait youth rooted in shared origins and devotion to the motherland, strengthened consensus on development in humanitarian and public-welfare fields, and encouraged more young people in Taiwan to learn about and visit Guizhou. It will further promote deeper and more substantive people-to-people exchanges and integration between Guizhou and Taiwan. The one-week summer camp brought participants to Guiyang, Anshun, Qiannan and Qianxinan Buyi and Miao Autonomous Prefectures. They visited Red Cross first-aid stations, studied Wang Yangming’s School of Mind, and experienced the enduring charm of fine traditional Chinese culture. Tours across Guizhou also enabled them to view landmark projects including the “Museum of World Bridges” and China’s Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope (FAST), and gain direct insights into Guizhou’s latest progress in economic, social, and scientific and technological innovation. (Jointly reported by Taiwan.cn and the Taiwan Affairs Office of Guizhou) Related Stories

item.title: For 14 Consecutive Years, Taiwan-Based Compatriot Grants Heartwarming Scholarship to Hometown Students
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-14
For 14 Consecutive Years, Taiwan-Based Compatriot Grants Heartwarming Scholarship to Hometown Students Source: Taiwan.cnUpdated: 2026-08-14
Aug 14(Taiwan.cn)—On August 13, the awarding ceremony for the "Tao Yuebo Hometown Youth Scholarship" was held at No. 2 High School of Xinzhou District, Wuhan. Tao Deyou, a Taiwan-based compatriot originally from Xinzhou, once again provided financial aid to college-bound students from his hometown, continuing an unbroken cross-Strait act of kindness for 14 years. At the ceremony, Tao Deyou, accompanied by his family, personally presented scholarships to seven eligible students this year, each receiving 4,000 yuan. While handing over the red envelopes, he urged the young recipients: "Study hard in college and grow into individuals who contribute to society." Tao Jun, Tao Deyou's niece, drove over 100 kilometers from Huangshi to attend the event and gave each scholarship recipient a custom-made red insulated mug. Staff members from the Huangshi Port-Area Committee of the Revolutionary Committee of the Chinese Kuomintang also offered each student a 500-yuan travel subsidy. Born in Taiwan, Tao Deyou pursued business careers in Hong Kong, South Africa, and elsewhere before retiring. During a trip back to his ancestral home in 2013, he learned that his grandfather had served as a school director of Zhengyuan Middle School, the predecessor of No. 2 High School of Xinzhou. In honor of his great-uncle, Tao Yuebo, he established the scholarship to support financially disadvantaged students admitted to universities. Despite the distance across the Taiwan Strait, this annual August promise has never faltered for 14 years. To date, more than 100 underprivileged students from No. 1, No. 2, and No. 4 High Schools of Xinzhou have benefited from the fund. Related Stories

item.title: Chinese mainland spokesperson slams Lai Ching-te's flattering remarks on Japan
item.description:
Published: 2026-02-11
Chinese mainland spokesperson slams Lai Ching-te's flattering remarks on Japan Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-02-11
BEIJING, Feb. 11 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday denounced Taiwan authorities led by Lai Ching-te for ignoring the heinous crimes committed by Japan during its colonial rule over Taiwan, describing their flattering remarks toward Japan as utterly disgraceful. Zhu Fenglian, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks in response to a media inquiry about Lai's intention to work with Japan to "deal with regional challenges." Zhu also urged the Japanese side to retract Sanae Takaichi's erroneous remarks on Taiwan, handle Taiwan-related issues prudently, and abide by the one-China principle with concrete actions. item.title: Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for obstructing cross-Strait exchanges
item.description:
Published: 2026-02-11
Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for obstructing cross-Strait exchanges BEIJING, Feb. 11 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson has condemned Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities for imposing restrictions and obstacles on cross-Strait exchanges in pursuit of their "Taiwan independence" agenda and selfish gains. The DPP authorities, led by Lai Ching-te, are the biggest obstacle to cross-Strait interactions and their acts have drawn strong criticism from various sectors in Taiwan, Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular press briefing on Wednesday. Zhu expressed the hope that Taiwan compatriots will firmly oppose the retrogressive actions of the DPP authorities and promote exchanges and cooperation across the Taiwan Strait in various fields. She noted that cross-Strait flight routes have been disrupted due to interference from the DPP authorities, with previously operated destinations yet to resume normal operations. In 2025, the average passenger load factor on cross-Strait routes reached 80 percent, reflecting the strong need for direct flights between the two sides of the Strait, Zhu said. "We hope that the Taiwan side will heed public opinion and lift unreasonable restrictions on cross-Strait air transport as soon as possible," she added.
